There are three levels of "code" in a lesson, from simplest to most interactive.

## 1. Static code

A normal fenced block is highlighted and gets a copy button. Add a filename and line numbers when you want to refer to specific lines.

```{.python filename="greet.py" code-line-numbers="true"}
def greet(name):
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

print(greet("Ada"))
```

## 2. Build-time execution

Fence with the language in braces and Quarto runs the code when it renders, then embeds the output. Learners see the result but cannot edit it.

````markdown
```{python}
squares = [n * n for n in range(1, 6)]
squares
```
````

This needs a Jupyter install (`python3 -m pip install jupyter`). The demo above is left unexecuted so this template renders with nothing but Quarto and PyYAML. For R, use the `knitr` engine with identical syntax: `{r}`.

## 3. Live, in-browser execution

For a course where learners edit and run code, add the **quarto-webr** extension. It runs a real R in the browser through WebAssembly, with nothing to install. The `rprogramming` course already uses it.

````markdown
---
engine: knitr
filters:
  - webr
---

```{webr-r}
x <- c(1, 2, 3)
mean(x)
```
````

::: {.callout-note}
## Turning this template into the R course
1. Copy this folder to `courses/rprogramming-v2/`.
2. Run `quarto add coatless/quarto-webr` inside it.
3. Add `engine: knitr` and `filters: [webr]` to lesson front matter (or once under `format.html` in `_quarto.yml`).
4. Port the old lessons: the quiz and "discuss first" markup is identical, so they paste straight in.
5. Copy `qwebr-force-dark.js` from the old course so the editor matches the dark theme.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="sm-quiz" data-quiz="mcq" data-answer="c">
  <p class="sm-quiz-q"><strong>Q1.</strong> Which option lets learners edit and run code themselves?</p>
  <div class="sm-quiz-options">
    <label><input type="radio" name="q-code-1" value="a"> A plain fenced code block</label>
    <label><input type="radio" name="q-code-1" value="b"> A build-time <code>{python}</code> cell</label>
    <label><input type="radio" name="q-code-1" value="c"> A quarto-webr cell</label>
  </div>
  <button class="sm-quiz-check">Check Answer</button>
  <div class="sm-quiz-feedback"></div>
</div>
```

::: {.takeaways}
- Static blocks show code, build-time cells show its output.
- quarto-webr makes R cells editable and runnable in the browser.
- Quiz markup is shared with the old R course, so lessons port unchanged.
:::
